title: Composing Components
description: Learn how to combine components to build complex user interfaces.

data.text: **Component composition** is the practice of assembling small, focused components into larger, more complex UIs. React's philosophy is composition over inheritance: build everything from small pieces rather than deep class hierarchies.

Think of React components like LEGO bricks. A button is a brick. A form is a structure built from buttons, inputs, and labels. A page is a structure built from forms, cards, and navbars. Each brick does one thing well.
React has a powerful composition model, and we recommend using composition instead of inheritance to reuse code between components.
A layout is a perfect composition example. Header, Sidebar, and Footer are independent components. The Page component composes them.

data.text: A general component can become specific through props. A generic Button component accepts variant, size, and onClick props. It does not need separate PrimaryButton and DangerButton components.

data.text: React identifies two main composition patterns: **containment** (using children) and **specialization** (using specific props to change behavior or appearance).

data.title: Keys Are Required
data.text: React warns if you omit keys in lists. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings. Avoid array indexes for lists that change.

items.question: Should I make a new component for every small piece?
items.answer: Aim for components with a single responsibility. If a piece has its own logic, state, or styling, it deserves its own file.

items.question: Can I nest components inside other components?
items.answer: Yes. Defining helper components inside a parent file is fine for small, private UI pieces.

items.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
items.answer: Composition builds UIs by nesting components. Inheritance creates a class hierarchy. React recommends composition because it is more flexible and easier to reason about.

items.question: How deep should my component tree go?
items.answer: As deep as needed for clarity. If passing props through 4+ levels becomes painful, consider Context or composition to collapse the tree.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Compose small components to build complex UIs.
Use children for containment and props for specialization.
Lists need stable keys so React can track items.
Favor composition over deep inheritance hierarchies.
data.takeaway: Composition is the heart of React. By mastering it, you can build any interface from simple, reusable building blocks.
